Starting with our meetings and systems. Whether it's team meetings to track data to make informed decisions about their respective school communities, or it's engaging with a family individual or some

kind of family meeting, our attendance team members are actively engaging in providing services and resources for our family. This is the foundation of our attendance work that decreases our chronic absenteeism, but also increases that Sense of Belonging amongst our students and families. From a state and a regional perspective in our practices, we meet monthly with our VDOE attendance representative.

In addition, we meet with all the attendance leaders from Region 4. So in those meetings, we're able to discuss best practices, receive attendance updates, and those meetings have been proven to be very helpful. Part of those meetings are the schools, the attendance officers, sometimes we have principals that attend those meetings. Also the Juvenile Court Services Unit, Loudoun County Mental Health, Department of Family Services. We're all at the table to make sure that we come together, we come up with resources and recommendations for the judge, so when the family does go to the disposition hearings, we have a report ready and recommendations to expedite those services and resources for our families and students.

Legal alignment, we meet with our Commonwealth Attorney's Office quarterly, just to make sure that we're in line with any new codes, but also to discuss truancy and attendance gaps that we may be having between our offices. In terms of agency collaboration, we are now meeting monthly with our Department of Family Services, Mental Health, and CPS, and Juvenile Court, and

discussing cases to make sure that we are aligned with our systems and discussing best practices. Restorative practices. Approximately three years ago, we started our Attendance and Engagement Circle. So it started as a pilot program. Last year, we opened it up to the whole school division. We had 13 schools that participated, having Attendance and Engagement Circles, and we saw increases in attendance engagement with those

students that attended those circles. Those circles are facilitated by teachers and Unified Mental Health Team members. Our judiciary best practice is team. This is a new collaboration, new team, that is led by Judge Kohler. He's one of our juvenile court judges. Ms. Evans and I had the opportunity to attend the first meeting, that was on August 18th. During that meeting, all the judges were present, the chief judge, Judge

Robinson, Judge Brooks, Commonwealth Attorney's Office, Public Defender's Office, the clerk of the court and juvenile court. Within this meeting, we were able to talk about some gaps that we're having between, particularly between schools and the courts. We were able to come up with some solutions, actually, within our first meeting. And I would say, within my 30 years of both working in the court system and the school system, this is the first time I've seen this level of transparency and

collaboration between the two systems, so it was a great start. Our family and community practices, we continue to collaborate with our FACE office and our Parent Educational Partners who provide services and presentations around chronic absenteeism and attendance awareness to those families that are part of those programs. Our Parent Coffee is just one of our ways that we engage parents

within our schools, but we do provide informal and formal sessions to our parents to raise awareness around attendance and just meeting them where they're at. So really, our community outreach is about meeting families where they're at, whether that's doing presentations at parks and rec centers, at the libraries, the juvenile courts. We go out and we do that community outreach to make sure that families are aware, but also that they're connected to the resources. Thank you.

And I will turn it over to Ms. Evans and Dr.- Okay, yeah, three. All right. Well, good evening Mrs. Accardi, Mr. Chernov, and Mr. Chandler. I am Shaheed Mohammed. I'm the acting assistant superintendent DEIA, if you didn't know. Just want to make sure. And I wanted to just give a little bit of overview of the connectedness of belonging and inclusion in this work, as well as

we will give some high-level overview of work that's being done in the division as we scale down to some of the great work that our esteemed principals will be sharing with you. So we want to differentiate belonging as a feeling versus inclusion as an action. So belonging is about feeling accepted, valued, and treated as a full member of a group. Inclusion is about what actions can be done to increase the likelihood that students will feel a sense of belonging, and that's

very important and key to this work. You will hear about the specific actions that the division is taking to support schools with attendance. Schools are taking action to create a culture of inclusion and to know and understand the individual needs of students and families for whom chronic absenteeism is an issue. I'm not going to read this slide to you, but you've heard from Dr.

Spence, and lots of our incredible various leaders within LCPS, that building and sustaining a strong sense of belonging in our students is everyone's responsibility. And belonging is a leading indicator, not a lagging indicator, for students' social, behavioral, and academic success. Addressing student absenteeism, as you well know, is a complex issue.

Creating and sustaining environments where students feel they belong is a factor that schools can leverage, and central office and school personnel can leverage and control. This slide and the next two slides will provide a high-level overview of the collaboration and work our schools, district offices, and entire school division does to actualize belonging for all students, and I'll turn it over to Jen.

Good evening. It's nice to see you all. On this slide, I really want to emphasize that we view schools as a sanctuary. When you talk about sense of belonging, you're really talking about connection, and all of us are responsible for ensuring that we offer that to our students and our families. That quote really resonated. That came out after the pandemic, which we're years away from now. But even just having that virtual connection, whether it's students during the

pandemic or whether they're doing asynchronous learning, whether they're having a video class, that connection is so important for us. And obviously, it's not nearly the same as actually being in a school building. You all have visited schools, and you feel it when you walk into our schools, that there's just that culture and that vibe in each of our buildings. So really, what is school connectedness? It's making sure that not only our students, but our families and our staff feel

cared for, supported, valued, and that they belong and have a place at the school. So it's a positive contributor for obvious reasons. When we see that kids have that sense of belonging, their attendance improves, their performance improves with their academics, and they thrive. So the research has really shown that it increases the healthier decision making, which are protective factors that we want all students to have, that they're making

responsible, healthy decisions as they grow. And they're more likely to have the achievement with higher grades, higher test scores, and overall better attendance. Next slide. You've seen this triangle again, just to emphasize that the things at that Tier 1 level are things that all students receive. And that is our Sources of Strength program, our prevention presentations with substance use, our counseling lessons,

our peer program, our Sources of Strength program, signs of suicide, substance use prevention. There's so much that goes into what's happening at the universal level for students. And then when you get to the Tier 2, Tier 3, those are our more targeted interventions when we identify issues and there's gaps, whether that's with connection or whether that's struggles outside of the school or even in school. That's where we do our targeted intervention across the academic,

behavioral, and social, emotional, mental health. We have Character Strong as evidence-based curriculum. We have other group curriculum that we provide to students, individual counseling services for students, and then if there's a crisis, we have our crisis response. And all throughout that, we're engaging with our families to ensure everyone's on the same page. So I really think it's a robust effort to make

sure that all of our students are seen and heard, but then when there are things that are not going well, that we're meeting them where they are and addressing the need and including their families. So we could go into all of those services. But I do want to end before I turn it over to Jen, is really when we talk about sense of belonging, we've heard a lot about the epidemic of loneliness. And really, it's not an epidemic of loneliness. It's an epidemic where we have a lack of connection.

So I really think that all of us working together, we're going to see and hear from our schools how much that can make a difference for a student and a family. Good evening. I'm Jen Short. I'm the principal at Sterling Elementary, and you can go to the next slide. You'll see on the screen our mantra, what we live by, every child, every day, whatever it takes. And we really do believe in this as a school. We serve a very precious community.

It's a very diverse community, and we have seen the need in our community grow over the years. I'm fortunate to be going into my 14th year there, and when I began, we were at about 35% free reduced lunch, and now we are one of the schools identified as having the highest percentage in the community eligibility provision that's published by the state. So that tells us that the belonging, like you heard my colleagues speak about, and school attendance is even more important, and we take that very seriously. You can go ahead to the next slide.

So as a school, we do invest heavily in belonging. To start our school year last year, that was one of the first things that we talked about coming off of Dr. Spence's keynote with us. That was one of the things that he really addressed. We took a look at what that does to student learning, and when students do feel connected, they are more inclined to take risks. We see that in our school, and they come to school. We also took a look even at the research.

In John Hattie's research, that effect size at .4, and it's just over that hinge point, so we know that we're really in that zone that we're aiming for when we're looking at the belonging. We also, as a school, have established what we call our Sterling Family Norms. So these are the things that we abide by as a staff. These are what we agree to when it comes to things like planning, our school community, but also how we interact with our children. And we agree as a staff that we're going to greet them at the door every single

day. So all administrators are outside every morning, and all teachers are at their door, making a point to seek the child out, use their name, assess how they're doing. If something's not going well, making sure that we're intervening right away. We also have our kindness ambassadors who we pair with students who begin after the school year starts, so they have an immediate connection. It's typically a child that's a year or two older than them, and often we try to pair children who speak the same language as well, especially if they're a

newcomer, just so they have a familiar face who can communicate with them to help them immediately get connected to the school. We lean into our office staff, too. If you've ever walked into our office, you know that they just do a great job of welcoming our community. But we chose to take the automated system off of our telephone, so it's always a person answering the phone. We always access their native language, and if we don't speak that in the office, then we access the language line. And little things like that, I think, make a

difference with our families and letting them know that they're seen here and they're valued, and we want them to engage with us. You can go ahead to the next slide. So I'll segue into the attendance piece, and I see it in several different pockets. The work that we do prior to the start of the school year, and then next I'll talk about the daily work, the biweekly, and the monthly work. But even prior to the start of the school year, over the summer, my social worker and I, we sit down and we look at our list of students who were chronically absent

the year prior. We have a target list that we have, and these are our students who we aim to connect with their families before the school year starts. So we call them in July, set up meetings in August, and have their families in to meet with us. Oftentimes too, we learn about different resources that they need, and we're able to connect them within the community or our school. We're intentional, too, in sharing the resources we have as administrators through attendance works, and really, I guess any school employee would be able to access

that or even any family. We also are intentional with our family communication. So I have a couple of slides that I give to our teachers and ask them to include in back-to-school nights. So we're all delivering the same message about when is a great time to stay home versus come to school. And then I ask for our staff to be really diligent in following through and pursuing our children if they're not here. We know in the research that our teachers are a big difference-maker in attendance.

As a principal and my social worker, we both have a role, but what we see in the research is the teacher's role is really the biggest deciding factor. So we ask that if children are absent two days in a row, that they reach out simply to say, "I missed you. We hope to see you soon." And then with three unexcused absences, they reach out to me, so we can start to work prior to what the state requires. We found it to be really helpful. You saw on an earlier slide the downward trend with our chronic absenteeism.

That first year that was presented there, mid-year, I discovered, and I don't know why I wasn't looking at it before, but I discovered that we were at about 25%, 26% of our students were chronically absent. So we started in January a big push, and we were able to decrease just below 15%, and we've just tried to capitalize on that movement since. You can go ahead to the next slide if you would. So thinking about our daily practices, I ask our registrar. She prints for me a daily attendance log.

I know who's come in, who's coming in late. Our students who are classified as McKinney-Vento, I know their patterns because there's some of them who they stop coming to school because they've moved, and they can't get here. So we are in relentless pursuit of them, making sure that they have what they need, and they're able to get to school. When kids return from an absence, we try to seek them out again to say, "So glad you're here today. Great job making it." And again, that focus on belonging and

active student engagement. We have also our Junior Jaguars, so students who maybe they're lagging in their attendance or in their interaction in the classroom, we pair a fourth or fifth grader with that student just to serve as a peer-to-peer mentor. So trying to utilize the strengths in our children within our building, and that really serves a purpose on both ends as well. Next slide, please. On a biweekly meeting, as you know, we meet with our attendance team. And at the elementary level right now for us, that consists of me, and when one of

my APs is available, she joins us, our school social worker, and our attendance officer. We take a look at our data in Click every single meeting. Usually by about late fall, I'm looking at in Click every day, just to know who's exactly where. We connect with our students who are in need of intervention. My social worker and I decide, all right, are we going to have a meeting with the students, or are we ready to bring in the family and have a meeting with the family? And we make that case-by-case determination. And then we also share out with our staff.

So I share out on a monthly basis the percentage by grade level in the same trends that were noted earlier, kindergarten and first grade being a little bit harder to get to school more regularly, until they learn the routine and the processes. And they also tend to be out with more illnesses. So we take a look at those trends and talk about those and call families. "Hey, I noticed that your child is coming to school more regularly. Thank you for making that adjustment." And we have found that to be helpful as well. And then for our students who we would classify as tier two or tier three, I

provide our teachers a script either to use on a phone call if they're in that tier three range, it's a phone call. If they're in tier two, it's an email that they send to them. So it's just less work for them, and they can just copy and paste or read right off of what we have there. And then finally, just a few other interventions to note. You heard, I think it was Darren mentioned the connection circles, the, I think, attendance and engagement circles, and we use them across all of the grade levels and find great success there. I mentioned the family meetings and our home visits.

We utilize an attendance tracker for select students that's color-coded, so they know when they're getting into the red, they need to make sure that they're here every day. Celebrating the improvements, shout-outs on the morning news show. Our attendance fairy makes a visit every month. The kids love that. And I do do family reminders to come back to school after a long weekend. We find that to be the best one. Did you share your attendance rate right now? It's just below 5%, yeah. Just making sure. I am the proud principal of Heritage High School in Leesburg, and I am excited to be here tonight to tell you a little bit about what we do at Heritage to increase belonging and increase that feeling of belonging with our

students and make sure that they know that they are connected. I think it does have an impact on attendance. Attendance at the high school is a pretty complex issue. We have also found that some of it is test avoidance, where students may be staying at home because they don't feel like

it's our mission this year to really focus in, much like Jen said, we're really hyper-focused on attendance a little bit more so this year. We have an incredible team. We work really well with our attendance officer, our student support advisor, as well as our student activities engagement coordinator. All work very closely together with the rest of our administration and

administrative leadership team to follow up with kids, make sure that we're doing all of the things with the letters and things like that. But we know that it requires more. So one of the things I'm doing on a monthly basis is including information for our parents and our families about why school attendance is so important, what students are missing out on. At Heritage, we are an IB school.

And our mission, you can see it there, is to ready all of our students for success and for what comes next for them. We've defined those things, and you can go to the next slide as well. We define those things using the terminology that you see there. That terminology comes from two places. It comes from the profile of the graduate for Virginia, as well as the International Baccalaureate Student Learner profile.

And we felt like it's very important for us to focus on those things. So much less on specific content knowledge and more so on whether students are prepared for what is going to happen after they leave Heritage. No matter what their choice is, no matter what their pathway is, whether it's military, whether it is college, whether it is an apprenticeship or immediately into the world of work. We want to value all of those, but those attributes are

ones that we know they will all need and will all help them be successful. And so you'll see there the things that we do to help students belong. And unfortunately, it also means that we're never really going to get to that perfect zone, but it does mean that

So as we're looking at our attendance, you can go to the next slide as well As we're looking at our attendance and as we're looking at how do we create a high school, a comprehensive high school, where students feel like they belong and they're connected, we do some things in a very deliberate way. For example, I'm out there greeting students in the morning. The rest of my administrative staff, we encourage people to be at their door, teachers to be at their door, not unlike what's happening at Sterling Elementary. We have a bell schedule with clubs incorporated into it. That is an outgrowth, and it's on the next slide as well, but that's an outgrowth of the work from staff, parents, students,

We celebrate our diversity that we have at Heritage. And then the student and staff leadership groups are constantly interrogating our culture and making sure that we're asking the right questions, that we're involving

our students in making leadership decisions so we can be intentional about making sure that students feel like they belong. You can go to the next slide. So that's just a sample. That's our bell schedule. Right? And so in the middle of our day, we have WIN time, and WIN stands for "What I Need." So it's What I Need time. On Mondays, we have Pride Time, which is our

advisory. On Tuesdays and Fridays, we have clubs. So it's 30 minutes where students can go and hang out with people who are sharing an interest, but it's not all focused on academics. And that is up 11.7 points in the past two years, so that also correlates to when we started this new bell schedule. And so that's been something that we've been really proud of. We definitely see the difference for our students.

We want you to belong. It's not just a feeling," but also we shared that data partly also to share with them that 87% said that they could be themselves, and 87% said, "Other students at this school care about me." And my point to them was, "That's not good enough. It needs to be closer to 100%." And so asking students to help me with that. So does that have a direct relationship to attendance? I think it probably has some relationship, right?

We saw the correlation based on the data. But it's something that without that, our attendance becomes that much more difficult to manage. up often. Yeah. Yeah, appreciate that, and I think that that's so insightful. They're going to be the ones that are going to be The ones that tell us what they're really feeling.
